clue.text: Particular way of thinking cares about film alien

parts.note: to mind something is to care about it, so 'cares about' gives the same verb in the same person
the stranded extraterrestrial of Spielberg's film, known by his two initials

explanation.surface: Somebody's settled opinion of a film about an alien.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' sits where a container instruction would and belongs to the verb in front of it. The alien is the one who wanted to phone home, and his two letters turn up in crosswords constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A mindset is the fixed set of attitudes somebody brings to everything, which is a particular way of thinking.

clue.text: Frightening horse seen around hansom

indicators.note: Something seen around another thing is on the outside of it, so the first word closes over the second.

parts.note: a mare is a female horse, and the word opens after two letters
a hansom is the two-wheeled horse-drawn cab of Victorian streets, so the word by itself asks for a cab

explanation.surface: A horse being walked round a hansom cab, and the sight is an alarming one.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse and hansom belong to the same Victorian street, which is what hides the seam between the two pieces. 'Hansom' is not the maker or the driver: the word means the cab itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Macabre describes whatever is gruesome enough to unsettle, the death-haunted end of frightening.

clue.text: Fine distinctions about island pests

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to lie all round it, so the word before closes over the letters after.

parts.note: nuances are fine shades of difference, and the word parts after two letters
is = island, the abbreviation printed on maps

explanation.surface: A scholarly quarrel over the finer points of some island's vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning' and is doing the placing instead. Pests here are people as easily as insects, which is the sense the plural answer carries.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuisance is anything or anybody that is a persistent irritation, which is what calling someone a pest says.

clue.text: Dismissal keeping 50 without a lot of work?

indicators.note: What a thing keeps it holds inside itself, so the numeral goes within the word.

parts.note: the sack is dismissal from a job, and the word opens after its first letter
l = fifty, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A sacking that somehow leaves fifty in hand and very little to do.
explanation.walkthrough: Roman fifty drops in one letter from the end of the front piece. The question mark is the setter conceding that a slack season is a loose way of saying there is not much work on.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade or a time of year called slack is one with little business going on, so work is thin.

clue.text: Hide art from this artist?

parts.note: the sentence first lands as a warning to keep your pictures away from somebody who cannot be trusted with them
hide is an animal's skin, and art worked on skin is the trade being described

explanation.surface: A warning to keep your pictures well out of one particular artist's reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' wants to be the verb and is the noun: a skin. The question mark flags that the whole sentence defines rather than any piece of it spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattooist's art goes permanently onto skin, and hide is skin, so the sentence reads straight as a description of the trade.

clue.text: Giant pig concealing rear end when reversing

indicators.note: To conceal a thing is to keep it out of sight inside, so one word closes over the other.
Anything reversing runs backwards, and the letters do the same, read from the far end.

parts.note: a hog is a pig, and it opens after its first letter
the rear end of an animal is its tail

explanation.surface: An enormous pig backing up and tucking its own behind out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The pig closes over its rear end, then the whole string runs backwards. The giant wanted is the Philistine champion of the Bible, brought down by a shepherd boy's sling.
explanation.definitionFit: Goliath was the giant David killed, and his name has become the ordinary word for anything hugely outsized.

clue.text: Look astonished about source of ripe fruit

indicators.note: To be about something is to sit round it, so the first word closes over the letter.
A word's source is where it starts, so only its opening letter is wanted.

parts.note: to gape is to stare open-mouthed, and the word opens after its first letter
the first letter of RIPE

explanation.surface: Somebody staring open-mouthed at the ripest fruit on the market stall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of ripe fruit' reads as one phrase — the vine — and only its last word defines. 'About' is placing the letter rather than meaning 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: A grape is the berry of the vine, so the bare word 'fruit' names its kind.

clue.text: Delicate garden item — indication of a bright idea?

parts.note: a light touch is a delicate one
the bulb planted in autumn for spring flowers

explanation.surface: Something fragile among the flowerbeds, and the cartoon sign that somebody has just thought of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicate garden item' reads as one description of a frail thing in the border and is two pieces bolted together. The dash marks the seam where spelling stops and defining starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Cartoons draw a light bulb over a character's head the instant they think of something, which is the bright idea meant.

clue.text: American tucking into a drink one more time

parts.note: the article is taken as a letter of the answer

indicators.note: To tuck into a thing is to get right inside it, so the letter goes within the word.

parts.note: gin is the drink, and it opens after its first letter
a = American, the dictionary's abbreviation

explanation.surface: An American getting stuck into a drink, and then having another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A drink' does two jobs at once: the article is a letter of the answer and the noun is the spirit that takes the insertion. The definition is the last three words, with no link word to announce it.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something again is to do it one more time, so the phrase swaps straight in for the adverb.

clue.text: Mostly horrible time in refuge

indicators.note: Mostly means all but the tail end, so the word gives up its final letter.

parts.note: HIDEOUS means horrible, docked of its last letter
t = time, the symbol in any physics formula

explanation.surface: A largely dreadful stretch of time spent somewhere safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly horrible time' reads as a grumble about a bad week and is an instruction, a word to dock and a letter. 'In' is grammar only; nothing is being put inside anything.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideout is where somebody on the run holes up, which is a refuge in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Major country's machinations partly revealed

indicators.note: Only part of what follows is shown, and the part shown is a run of its letters sitting where they already are.

parts.note: the letters run on inside MACHINATIONS, starting one letter in

explanation.surface: A great power's scheming, with only some of it out in the open.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place is a single long word rather than a run of short ones, which is the hardest kind to spot. Everything after the definition is one lump of letters plus the instruction to look inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: China is one of the world's largest countries by population, area and economy, so 'major country' names it by rank.

clue.text: Rip apart good ground? It produces signs of sadness

parts.note: to rip something apart is to tear it
g = good, the grade on a school report
land is the ground underfoot

explanation.surface: An order to break up a decent patch of soil, and a note on what makes people cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apart' looks like the instruction to jumble whatever follows; it belongs to 'rip' instead, and the two words together are one synonym. The question mark marks the seam where the spelling stops.
explanation.definitionFit: The tear gland above the eye makes the tears that show when somebody is upset, so it produces the visible signs.

clue.text: Support accepting source of light? Difficulty — this emits no light

indicators.note: Whatever accepts a thing takes it in, so the letter goes inside the word.
A word's source is its beginning, so its first letter alone is taken.

parts.note: to back somebody is to support them, and the word opens after its first letter
the first letter of LIGHT
the hole you are in is the difficulty you are in

explanation.surface: A prop taking in a little light, and the trouble of a place with none at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' appears twice and only the first one pays out a letter; the second belongs to the definition. 'Difficulty' looks like a comment on the clue and is the second spelling piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A black hole's gravity is strong enough that not even light escapes it, so nothing at all comes out.

clue.text: Beat and energy in dance

parts.note: to tan somebody is to thrash them, the sense in 'tan your hide'
go is the energy in 'plenty of go left in him'

explanation.surface: A rhythm and some vigour out on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' sounds like the pulse the dancers move to and is the violent sense instead. 'In' is grammar only, joining the spelling to the definition without putting anything inside anything.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is the Argentine ballroom dance, so the bare word 'dance' names its kind.

clue.text: Fish: catching 90, do well

indicators.note: To catch a thing is to take hold of it and keep it, so the numeral ends up inside the word.

parts.note: the eel is the crossword's standing fish, and it opens after its first letter
xc = ninety in Roman numerals, a hundred with ten taken off the front

explanation.surface: A fish landing a catch of ninety and thriving on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the job a link word would, separating the word to be opened from the instruction. Roman ninety is written by subtraction, which is why it starts with an X.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to do something notably well, better than those around you.

clue.text: Stupidest, nevertheless, in America

definitions.note: 'Stupidest' defines the entry read as two words, while the grid takes it as one.
definitions.meaning: the superlative of not being clever, which wants two words where the grid has one
run together it is the American and dialect adverb for anyway or at any rate

explanation.surface: The daftest of the bunch, or so they would put it over in America.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'nevertheless' is the join between two separate definitions, not a pause inside one sentence. The first works only because the answer falls apart into two ordinary words.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two the answer reads 'least wise', which is stupidest; run together it is the American and dialect word for nevertheless or at any rate.

clue.text: I'm a puritan, not heartless, but unwise

indicators.note: Something heartless has had its middle taken out, so the word loses its central letter.

parts.note: the two letters of the contraction, apostrophe dropped
a prude is the puritan about morals and manners
NOT with its middle letter taken away

explanation.surface: A self-declared puritan insisting there is nothing cold about them.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a confession and every word of it before the last is spelling. 'Not heartless' is the denial in the sentence and the instruction in the wordplay: the word NOT loses its own heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody imprudent acts without weighing the consequences, which is unwise in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Leader's power given to citizen

parts.note: p = power, the symbol in physics
a resident is whoever lives in the place, its citizen

explanation.surface: A leader handing their authority over to an ordinary citizen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader's power' reads as one phrase and only the first word defines; the apostrophe-s is the link. The surface has the powerful giving power away, which is the last thing the answer suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A president heads a republic or an organisation, so 'leader' names the office by what it does.

clue.text: Eliminate idea and react strangely

indicators.note: Letters behaving strangely are not in the order they were handed over in, so they have to be resorted.

parts.note: the nine letters of IDEA and REACT, re-sorted

explanation.surface: Killing off a thought and then behaving oddly about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eliminate idea' reads as one instruction and only the first word defines; the idea is raw material. 'And' joins the two words being jumbled, not two separate pieces of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To eradicate something is to root it out entirely, which is eliminating it.

clue.text: Take apart battered tin medals

indicators.note: Something battered has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape come back in a new order.

parts.note: the nine letters of TIN MEDALS, re-sorted

explanation.surface: Dented tin medals being pulled to bits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' sits exactly where a solver expects an adjective describing the medals, which is why it reads past as scenery. The definition describes what the anagram is doing to its own letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle something is to take it to pieces part by part, which is taking it apart.

clue.text: Seemly behaviour heading off public meeting after last month

indicators.note: Heading off takes the head away, so the word loses its first letter.
'After' fixes the order rather than joining: the piece in front of it is set behind the one named next.

parts.note: December is the last month of the year, in the three-letter form used on calendars
a public meeting is a forum, beheaded

explanation.surface: Walking out of a public meeting held since the end of last month.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's order is the reverse of the answer's: 'after' sends the month to the front. 'Heading off' reads as leaving early and is the instruction to dock a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorum is the propriety an occasion calls for, so it is behaviour that is seemly.

clue.text: Unexciting line penned by group

indicators.note: To be penned by something is to be shut in by it, so the letter sits inside the word.

parts.note: a band is a group of musicians, and the word opens after its first letter
l = line, the abbreviation on a map or a timetable

explanation.surface: A dull line of verse shut in by the band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penned by' pulls towards the pen that writes, which suits the line of verse; the pen that keeps sheep in is the one meant. Line is one of the commonest single letters in the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bland has no flavour or character to it, which is what calling it unexciting says.

clue.text: Ruin of the French city of antiquity

parts.note: 'of the' in French, before a plural noun, is des
Troy, the besieged city of Homer's Iliad, dug up on the Turkish coast

explanation.surface: The wreck of some ancient French city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of the French' asks for the French for 'of the', the same trick as 'the French' for LE. The city is Homer's, on the Turkish coast, and has nothing French about it.
explanation.definitionFit: To destroy something is to ruin it beyond repair, so the two verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: Wagon carrying a measure of gold

indicators.note: What a wagon carries rides inside it, so the letter goes within the word.

parts.note: a cart is the wagon, and it opens before its last letter
the article taken as a single letter

explanation.surface: A wagon hauling a load of gold away.
explanation.walkthrough: The load being carried is one letter, the article, which is why so little goes inside. The measure wanted is the one out of twenty-four that states how pure gold is.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold purity is given in carats out of twenty-four, so the carat is literally a measure of gold.

clue.text: Turn away and show astonishment about start of play

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to be wrapped round it, so the word closes over the letter.
The start of a word is its opening letter and nothing more.

parts.note: to reel is to stagger, which is what a shock does to somebody
the first letter of PLAY

explanation.surface: Staggering backwards at the opening of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of play' is a cricket commentator's phrase pressed into service as a single letter. Reeling is astonishment shown with the whole body, which is why a verb of staggering answers a verb of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel somebody is to drive them back, which is turning them away from you.

clue.text: Formal sign in US elections

parts.note: prim means stiffly formal and proper
Aries the Ram, the first sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A stiffly worded placard at an American election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' has nothing to do with placards: it is the zodiac, where crosswords take the word nearly every time. 'In' is grammar rather than a container instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: American parties choose their candidates in primaries, the state-by-state votes held before the election proper.

clue.text: Gospel character I omitted in part of service

indicators.note: What is omitted is left out altogether, so the letter named in front of it never appears.

parts.note: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor in the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion
the letter dropped out of his name

explanation.surface: A figure from the Gospels who was left out of the service.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' is a bare letter, not the Roman numeral or the pronoun it looks like. Both senses of 'service' work: the dinner set and the church collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A plate is one item of a dinner service, and the plate passed round for the collection is part of a church service too.

clue.text: A farm crop is source of much growth

parts.note: the clue's first word taken as a letter
corn is the farm's cereal crop, wheat in Britain and maize in America

explanation.surface: A field crop that turns out to be where a great deal of growing begins.
explanation.walkthrough: The very first word of the clue is a letter of the answer, which is easy to read straight past. 'Source of much growth' is the proverb about great oaks in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: The acorn is the oak's seed, and great oaks from little acorns grow, so a very large amount of growth starts there.

clue.text: Copy broadcast of later epic

indicators.note: To broadcast in the older farming sense is to fling seed far and wide, and letters flung about land in a new order.

parts.note: the nine letters of LATER EPIC, re-sorted

explanation.surface: A repeat showing of some later epic film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like a signal about sound and is the scattering sense instead, which is an anagram and never a homophone. 'Copy broadcast' reads as one phrase and splits between the definition and the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To replicate something is to make a copy of it, so the verbs swap straight over.

clue.text: Broadcasting extract from Siberian orchestra in reverse

indicators.note: Whatever is extracted from something was already sitting inside it, so the letters are a run taken straight out of the words that follow.
In reverse means back to front, so the run is read from its last letter to its first.

parts.note: the run RIANO starts four letters from the end of SIBERIAN and takes the O of ORCHESTRA, then is read backwards

explanation.surface: A clip of a Siberian orchestra being played backwards on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden runs seldom travel backwards as well, so the letters are out of sight twice over. The break falls inside a word rather than at a space, which is what keeps the run invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that is on air is going out to listeners at that moment, which is broadcasting.

clue.text: Island resident, a man, holding group back

indicators.note: What a man holds is inside his grasp, so the second word goes within the first.

parts.note: a male is a man, and the word opens before its last letter

indicators.note: Taken back, a word is read from its end to its beginning.

parts.note: a set is a group of things taken together

explanation.surface: An islander holding a crowd back from getting through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding ... back' looks like one phrase about restraint and is two instructions, one to contain and one to reverse. Malta is the small island state in the Mediterranean, south of Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: A Maltese is somebody from Malta, so the answer names an islander by the island.

clue.text: Leather producer woman featured in essay

indicators.note: To be featured in something is to appear inside it, so the name goes within the word.

parts.note: to essay something is to try it, the verb rather than the schoolwork
Anne, one of the handful of women's names setters reach for when they need four letters

explanation.surface: A leather-maker and a woman who both turn up in somebody's essay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' is the verb, to attempt, and the noun reading is the whole of the misdirection. Any short woman's name is fair for the insides, so the crossing letters are what settle which one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tannery is the works where raw hides are tanned into leather, so leather is what it produces.
